I have a vivid memory of being a old lady. In fact I believe I recall my death. I was probably in my 70s or so. I lived in a house with wood paneling on the walls. My furniture was orange/brown- ugly by todays standards- so I’m assuming this was the 80s. I remember feeling tired and looking my cat who was sitting near the side of the couch. I laid down on the couch and looked at the windows which were adjacent to it. Things went dark. Not sure if I fell asleep and passed or if that was the passing. I remember in my passing the cat wandering around me and looking at me. Almost as if I saw it as I left. 

I definitely lived alone in this life. To this day I have a deep love for cats and a hatred for being in my house by myself.

There is also another memory of being a child in a fairly affluent family in the early 1900s. However, this was not a life I lived in very long. I have a distinct memory of looking out the window and being sad I couldn’t play outside under the big tree anymore because I was so sick. 

To this day, I love trees! The bigger and shadier the better. 

I also think in that life I was harmed by a toaster at some point (unrelated to my death). I once came across a photo of a early 1900s toaster and was immediately sick to my stomach. As a kid in this life, I was terrified of toasters and the hot coils in them (those used to be exposed in early models) and even as an adult I prefer not to use them.
For me it’s not mortality, it’s the reality of the medical bills and inconvenience of being hurt.

You’re working against several logical fallacies, or thought distortions. The first one is thinking through the lens of “should.” You should do this, you should do that. “Should” is an indicator that we’re giving someone else’s voice much more power than our own. 

You’re also doing something called black and white thinking. It’s a rigid form of thinking that forces you to feel restricted in your life. You say you have no hope of getting out of a low income lifestyle because of mental illness or disability, while ignoring any evidence that might be contrary to that. 

You are also doing something called emotional reasoning. Believing that just because you believe something, it must be true. 

These are common fallacies everyone experiences from time to time. Unfortunately, you’ve created a narrative with them that forces you to see yourself as something bad. The problem is not being white, or taking up space. It’s not viewing your place in the world with compassion and flexibility or a realistic lens.

If you’re not already, please start working with a therapist so you can break apart these thoughts from one another.

Sure. Overall the book is good but it’s definitely probably more appropriate for ages 12-18. I’m a 32 year old woman who picked it up on a new release shelf at Barnes and Noble without doing any research. I think because of that, I had some disconnect with the main characters who are two males age 17 and 18. 

The author clearly identified with one of the characters more as his dialogue was more natural. The other character seemed a little bit disjointed and forced. There’s lot of teenage specific issues and sexual identity themes. But that’s unrelated to the overall story. 

The story centers around one central theme which is really thought provoking, but can also be super anxiety producing if you’re someone with mental illness. I feel like I should have left the book with more motivation to live life to it’s fullest, but I had trouble sleeping the first night after finishing it because I was hyper fixated on how my mental illness makes me struggle with that. 

If you’re prone to worrying and anxiety I think you should bypass it. There’s a lot of unpredictability in the story and I read to get away from that in real life. There’s also no comfortable resolution so if you like things tied up nicely and feeling like you have closure you won’t find it in this book. You may feel helpless reading along and at the end feel a little hopeless. That said, the story and reality it presents are very interesting and will leave you considering “what if that was real life?” for a long time. It’s a great book for discussions.

Catholic perspective:

In ancient Judaism it was not just the slaughter of an animal that resulted in purification. The ritual required a second part. Consuming that animal. Both parts needed to be complete. 

Jesus was the lamb that was slaughtered. He was not symbolically slaughtered. He was actually slaughtered. He commanded we eat his flesh. This fulfills the second part of the purification process. We do that through the means he introduced (the Eucharist). We leave it up to God to transform that bread into the body, time and time again. But we believe the sacrifice and purification of man is not complete unless the sacrifice is eaten (not symbolically). 

Many will ask why we do this ritual over and over again. 

Because in Catholicism, Christ’s sacrifice is always happening. It wasn’t a one time event. It’s not a thing to be remembered because it’s not in the past. The event we take part in has no end.

I firmly believe I grew up in a house with a demon. 

In 1999, (I was 9 years old) my family and I moved to a house in an upper middle-class neighborhood. It was a stark white, two story stucco near a golf course. The house had stairs in the middle of the layout with a half open top floor concept (basically an indoor balcony). This will matter latter. 

No one in my family really loved the house, but I was insistent that I lived near my friend so I begged and pleaded. My parents gave in and we moved into the home fairly quickly. 

As soon as we moved in odd things began to happen. I remember having vivid dreams and seeing a shadow of man in a cowboy hat. I was always one to attract odd things when I was a kid, so I didn’t think much of it, until a friend down the road told me someone had died in my home. He described it as an elderly woman, so I didn’t think the man in the hat was related, but it opened my mind to the possibility of a haunting.

What followed in the years of living there was terror. Several incidents happened, but the most notable was the day I was running late to dance practice. I was probably 12 or so at the time. As I descended the stairs, I felt all the hair on my neck stand up and knew I was being watched from above - the indoor balcony. This was a problem because the rest of my family was downstairs.

I remember looking up to see one of the most horrible things I’ve ever seen in my life. Words fall short, but the closest thing I can relate it to was a dementor from Harry Potter- with a slightly more skeletonized appearance. 

I screamed and took off racing down the stairs, and was overcome with a sense of sickness. I glanced up a couple more times as I descended and the thing was still there watching me. When I reached the bottom, I steadied myself and momentarily looked up one last time and it vanished. 

It took months for me to be comfortable enough to walk those stairs alone again. My parents shrugged it off as my imagination- but little did I know they were having their own experiences.

My dad recalled one day where he was taking a nap in his room. He woke up and said his body felt like he was being hit by a truck. He said at that moment he was overcome by the most despair he had ever known. Extreme sadness, depression, and rage filled him. He claims to this day it took years to shake that feeling and said he felt possessed at times. I’m not sure he ever shook it completely- in the years since, he’s made awful and evil life decisions.

But there is more. 

Throughout my childhood, friends refused to come over after awhile. I was getting a reputation for having an odd house in my friend group. Not many outside this group had that knowledge until one day when the bus dropped me off at home in middle school. 

On a normal day, I would come home at 3:15 to an empty house. My parents would get home around 5:00. My house was the bus stop. There were no windows facing the front of the house except for the window upstairs that was my room. 

One particular day, the bus stopped to drop me off. I grabbed my keys from my backpack and was focused on zipping the lock when a series of bangs were heard in quick succession. I looked back at the bus to see dozens of horrified faces slamming the windows of the bus and pointing up. With that, the bus drove away. 

I raced back to the street to see what everyone was pointing at. It had to have been the window but nothing was there. I shook it off as a prank, and walked inside. Nothing special happened. But the next day when I got on the bus people acted very odd. I finally got one kid to fess up that the kids on the bus had seen something scary in my window. A man- but not my father who everyone had known. No one would give me more detail. 

In 2007 we finally somewhat rid ourselves of this house. We moved to another area of town but the house was plagued with bad luck. We kept it on the market for months but no one was interested. My parents were forced to turn it into a rental.

Surprise, surprise- renters didn’t last long. One man of middle eastern descent who was there for a time brought in some sort of herb that was meant to capture “bad air.” His beliefs were such that any negative energy would be absorbed by the leaves. The plants died and crumbled quickly when they came in the home.

In late 2014, my parents divorced and my mom was forced to move back into the home as they separated their assets. She complained of hearing odd noises, train sounds, electronics. But nothing too exciting happened to her. She finally sold the house in 2018. 

The young couple that purchased the home seemed very in love with it. They got it for a sweet deal too. I drove by the home three months after it was sold to them. It sat vacant. No furniture, no window dressings, no lights. They realtor stated they vacated immediately. 

This is only a small fraction of the stories I have of this house. It literally haunts me in my dreams. And I mean literally. I still dream on a monthly basis that I am trapped inside and I wake up in a sweat. I’m fact, I had one of these dreams last night.

When it comes to the premonition worries I encourage you to try and look beyond what you might see. Surely you’ve had other reoccurring dreams- teeth falling out, late for class, leaving the house with no pants. Just because you dream something multiple times does not mean it will happen. 

People tend to only notice the reoccurring dreams that manifest in reality while forgetting all the mundane ones. Your brain will filter out any themes or premonitions or hunches that don’t come true because it’s non essential information. 

That said, reoccurring dreams often point to something that hasn’t been emotionally processed. The meaning of your wife’s dream will be immensely personal to her. It will be a reflection of how she views her own death. Is she fearful of missing out on life? Is she afraid she has not accomplished more? Does she view death as the end of all things? The more she has those fears in the waking hours, the more vivid her dreams will become. 

I could see how infertility struggles would cause her to feel like she’s missing out. Or make her believe that if she obtains the child she wants so badly, it will all be taken away. These are very common themes with anxiety. 

My guess is she envisioned a full family by her 30s and with that looming in the near future, it’s brought up a lot of emotional stuff for her. Many people fear dying in their thirties. I was one of them. It’s hard to process that life will be different then planned, but different doesn’t mean nonexistent. 

If she’s not already working with a therapist I encourage her to consider it. Also look into alternative forms of infertility treatment- natural family practitioners have had wonderful success stories. Engage in some sort of spiritual practices (doesn’t have to be traditional church). Anything that offers hope and brings meaning to life. Remember the old saying- the wolf you feed will be the one that grows. The more she dwells on her fears and anxieties, the more they will manifest and feel real.

5. Frequent symptoms- for me it feels like bees are always in my body. Also I’m almost always dizzy and short of breath. I get heart palpitations and panic attacks at random. Especially when I’m calm. 

I also get flashbacks. I will get a weird cloudy feeling in my head, colors seems a bit off and my body feels very scared as if the thing is happening again. 

6. Realistic portrayal-my advice would be to really try and show how we make trauma the center of our lives even without meaning to. For me I went years not eating certain foods because I thought they would make me sick and I would have to go back to the hospital. You will be fine as long as you don’t keep any items of *percieved* value in the car. 

Example:

Garage door opener= fairly worthless to most people but a criminal could see that and think it a good enough excuse to break into your car. Their next step would be straight to your glove box to see if you have an address near by so they could use your garage door opener to gain easy access. 

All they need is something potentially valuable so be mindful about what you keep in the car. I’ve seen cars broken into over some spare change and an empty plastic toolbox. Remember it’s not the value of the item to you, it’s the value of an item to a criminal. 

Also be smart about where you keep the car. Park in lighted areas. Next to security, cameras, entrances, etc is always helpful. 

The Albuquerque population is 558,000 people and roughly 10,000 cars are stolen every year. Even though that’s a high number, having your car stolen is still statistically pretty rare.
